newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian political rivals join hands to court Iran.
newsitem.headline: Russian political rivals join hands to court Iran.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin and his political opponents on Friday joined forces in courting Iran despite a German court ruling that Tehran was responsible for state terrorism.

Yeltsin, who met visiting Iranian parliament chief Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, offered "to strengthen and develop" bilateral ties, while the head of the lower house of the Russian parliament said the Berlin court had no right to take a whole country to trial.
"We have good, positive co-operation with Iran, which shows a tendency to grow," a smiling Yeltsin told the white-bearded, turbaned Iranian.

Russia has been seeking to diversify its foreign policy partners at a time when Western Europe is ignoring Moscow's protests and going ahead with plans to expand the NATO alliance into eastern Europe.
Yeltsin's public call for closer ties with Iran put him decidedly out of step with Western countries including the United States, which calls Iran a sponsor of international terrorism.
Germany expelled four Iranian diplomats on Thursday after a Berlin court announced its conclusion that Iran had ordered the 1992 murders of Kurdish activists in Berlin.

The court said a secret special operations committee whose members included Iran's president, its religious leader, intelligence minister and the head of foreign policy had ordered the assassination of four Kurdish Iranian leaders in 1992.
The European Union, which Moscow said last month it wanted to join, suggested after the verdict that member countries recall their ambassadors from Iran "for consultations".
The Duma chairman, communist Gennady Seleznyov, told a joint news conference with Nateq-Nouri that the Western rebuff had not affected the Iranian's talks in Moscow.

Seleznyov said the conservative legislature, which has no role in shaping foreign policy, did not differ with Yeltsin and his government on foreign policy, although they disagree on many other issues.
"We are now re-establishing comprehensive ties with...our old allies," he said.

Seleznyov also issued veiled criticism of a German court verdict on Iran. "One can take a person to court for a crime he has committed but there is no court in the world which has the authority to pass sentence on a whole nation," he said.
Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, a Middle East specialist appointed last year, has made better relations with this region and the rest of Asia a policy priority.

Moscow announced on Thursday it would host Chinese President Jiang Zemin later this month for a visit designed to build the foundations for closer ties after decades of mutual distrust following border clashes in the 1960s.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda visited Moscow last month.
Russia also sees considerable commercial and diplomatic opportunity in Iran, and is building a nuclear power plant there despite strong U.S. objections.
